title: Planning a Production-Ready Pipeline knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Planning a Production-Ready Pipeline?
options: Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
Plan a production-ready pipeline by defining the outcome, supported runtimes, quality gates, trust boundaries, artifact flow, deployment stages, and recovery evidence.
questions.answer_key: Plan a production-ready pipeline by defining the outcome, supported runtimes, quality gates, trust boundaries, artifact flow, deployment stages, and recovery evidence.
questions.explanation: This is the central behavior of planning a production-ready pipeline: Plan a production-ready pipeline by defining the outcome, supported runtimes, quality gates, trust boundaries, artifact flow, deployment stages, and recovery evidence. Validate configuration and behavior against the current official reference before production use.

questions.prompt: A team is working with “Translating project requirements into workflow requirements”. Which practice best fits this topic?
options: Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.
Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
questions.answer_key: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.
questions.explanation: Translating project requirements into workflow requirements: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action. Apply the guidance to the actual event, runner, permissions, or artifact boundary and test the relevant case.

questions.prompt: How should a reviewer verify a change related to planning a production-ready pipeline?
options: Assume the workflow is correct as soon as the YAML file is committed.
Retry every failure without looking at the exit code or preserving evidence.
Publish the workflow to production before reviewing its triggers and permissions.
Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.answer_key: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Reliable verification uses observable evidence. For this lesson, consider: Plan a production-ready pipeline by defining the outcome, supported runtimes, quality gates, trust boundaries, artifact flow, deployment stages, and recovery evidence. A syntax check alone cannot prove remote execution, permissions, or deployment behavior.
